core_summary: This chapter covers the end-to-end data processing workflow: collection of raw data, organization using tally mark frequency tables, visual representation via pictographs with unit scales, construction of accurate bar graphs, and critical interpretation of visual data to detect misleading graphs.
key_concepts: Data Organization via Tallies: Tally marks record individual observations; every 5th count is drawn as a diagonal slash across four vertical tallies ('||||/') to create bundles of 5.
Frequency Distribution: Frequency quantifies how many times a specific observation value occurs within a dataset.
Pictograph Scale Keys: A pictograph represents counts using symbols, where 1 icon represents a declared key scale value. Fractional icons denote proportional partial values.
Bar Graph Construction Rules: Rectangular bars must have uniform width, equal spacing between adjacent bars, and a vertical scale starting from a clear baseline 0.
Scale Calculation: Bar height in centimeters equals Category Frequency divided by Scale Quantity per centimeter.
Detecting Misleading Graphs: Truncating the vertical axis (not starting at 0) artificially exaggerates bar height differences, misleading visual interpretation.

key_terms.definition: An unorganized collection of initial facts, figures, measurements, or observations.
The total integer count of times a specific data value or category occurs in a dataset.
A visual representation of categorical data using picture icons governed by a declared scale key.
A chart using parallel rectangular bars of uniform width whose lengths/heights are proportional to frequency.
The fixed quantitative value assigned to 1 unit length on a graph axis or 1 icon in a pictograph.

key_takeaways: Organizing raw data into frequency tables is essential for drawing meaningful mathematical inferences.
Uniform bar width and equal spacing maintain visual integrity in data graphics.
A zero baseline on vertical axes is mandatory to prevent visual distortion of proportions.
